Shock, altered mental status, oliguria or other sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
Multilobar disease, cavitation or a large pleural effusion
Immunocompromise, aspiration risk or failure to improve on appropriate initial therapy
symptoms: Acute cough with or without sputum
Fever, rigors or malaise
Dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain
Confusion or functional decline, especially in older adults

Fever or hypothermia with tachycardia
Confusion, hypotension or poor perfusion in severe disease

Orthopnoea, bilateral congestion, raised jugular venous pressure and cardiac dysfunction.
Diffuse upper-respiratory features without focal consolidation or compatible chest imaging.
Subacute constitutional symptoms, epidemiologic risk, upper-lobe or cavitary change and specific microbiology.

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is infection of the distal airways and alveoli acquired outside hospital or early after admission. Alveolar inflammation and exudate impair ventilation and gas exchange; systemic inflammatory effects may cause sepsis and organ dysfunction.
keyMechanisms: Pathogen aspiration or inhalation overcomes airway and innate immune defences.
Alveolar neutrophilic inflammation and fluid cause consolidation and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Host response varies with age, comorbidity, immune status and pathogen virulence.
Complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure and sepsis.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess severity
actions: Assess oxygenation, sepsis features, comorbidity and ability to take oral treatment.
Use a validated severity tool as an adjunct, not a replacement for clinical judgement.
Identify aspiration, resistant-organism, travel and immunocompromise risks.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Start empiric antimicrobial therapy
actions: Select generic therapy from the current MOH/local formulary according to severity, allergy, recent exposure and the local antibiogram.
Obtain indicated cultures first only when this will not delay urgent therapy.
Document indication, route, review date and planned duration.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after diagnosis; immediately when sepsis or shock is present

clinicalManagement.title: Provide supportive care
actions: Titrate oxygen to the appropriate clinical target.
Treat sepsis, fluid deficit, pain and fever while accounting for cardiac and renal status.
Provide thrombosis prevention and early mobilisation for admitted patients when appropriate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Concurrent with antimicrobial treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Review response and complications
actions: Reassess observations, oxygen need, mental status, oral intake and inflammatory/organ-function trends.
Narrow or change antimicrobials using microbiology and clinical response.
Investigate empyema, abscess, resistant pathogen, obstruction or an alternative diagnosis when improvement is absent.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Formal review within 24 to 48 hours or sooner if deteriorating

clinicalManagement.title: Switch route and plan discharge

Use the shortest effective guideline-concordant course and document the stop date.
Arrange follow-up imaging only for persistent symptoms or guideline-defined risk, not automatically for every patient.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When clinically stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange clinical review based on severity and comorbidity; follow pending cultures, reassess non-resolution, and consider interval chest imaging for persistent symptoms or higher malignancy risk according to local policy.

Microbiology or infectious diseases for resistant organisms, severe immunocompromise or treatment failure

Offer smoking-cessation support.
Review influenza, pneumococcal and other indicated vaccination after recovery.

Give return precautions for worsening breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, chest pain or inability to maintain intake.
Explain antimicrobial adherence and why unused antibiotics should not be saved or shared.

The patient can take oral medicine and maintain hydration and nutrition.
A safe antimicrobial plan, follow-up ownership and return precautions are documented.

content.title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Haematology

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with persistent hypotension or obstructive-shock features
Severe hypoxaemia, rapidly escalating oxygen requirement or cardiac arrest
Threatened limb with massive swelling, cyanosis or severe pain
Active major bleeding or another absolute barrier to anticoagulation in a patient with confirmed or highly suspected VTE
symptoms: Unilateral leg pain or swelling
Sudden unexplained dyspnoea
Pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis or syncope
Reduced exercise tolerance with recent immobility, surgery, cancer or prior thrombosis
physicalSigns: Unilateral pitting oedema, calf asymmetry or deep venous tenderness
Tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxaemia
Signs of right-heart strain such as raised jugular venous pressure
Hypotension or poor perfusion in high-risk pulmonary embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema, warmth and a possible portal of entry with inflammatory features rather than isolated deep venous tenderness.
Posterior knee pathology with fluid tracking into the calf and diagnostic ultrasound findings.
Pressure-type pain, ischaemic electrocardiographic change or a coronary biomarker pattern rather than pleuritic pain and right-heart strain.
Focal infective symptoms or unilateral absent breath sounds with confirmatory chest imaging.

ruleIn.testName: Compression ultrasonography
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Compression ultrasonography — Proximal lower-limb DVT
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Non-compressible venous segment or directly visualised thrombus.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: First-line anatomical confirmation for suspected proximal DVT.

ruleIn.testName: CT pulmonary angiography
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT pulmonary angiography — Pulmonary embolism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intraluminal filling defect in a pulmonary artery.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms pulmonary embolism and describes clot burden while also identifying some alternative thoracic diagnoses.

ruleIn.testName: Echocardiography in unstable PE
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography in unstable PE — Right-ventricular pressure overload
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Right-ventricular dilatation or dysfunction compatible with acute pressure overload.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports urgent risk stratification when instability makes definitive imaging unsafe or delayed.

ruleOut.testName: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway — Acute VTE
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A negative result below the assay's validated threshold makes acute VTE unlikely in the selected population.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute VTE
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids unnecessary imaging only after structured clinical-probability assessment.

ruleOut.testName: Ventilation-perfusion imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Ventilation-perfusion imaging — Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal perfusion argues strongly against PE; a mismatched perfusion defect supports it.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Provides an alternative when contrast, radiation distribution or renal considerations make CTPA unsuitable.

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism results from venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. A deep-vein thrombus may obstruct limb venous return or embolise to pulmonary arteries, increasing dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance and, in severe cases, causing right-ventricular failure and shock.
keyMechanisms: Thrombus formation is promoted by immobility, surgery, cancer, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy and inherited or acquired thrombophilia.
Pulmonary arterial obstruction produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can reduce left-ventricular filling and systemic cardiac output.
Residual venous obstruction and valve damage contribute to post-thrombotic syndrome; persistent vascular obstruction may cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

clinicalManagement.title: Estimate clinical probability
actions: Use a validated DVT or PE clinical-probability tool within its intended population.
Check haemodynamic stability and bleeding risk before selecting the diagnostic pathway.
Do not use a D-dimer to rule out VTE when clinical probability is high.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain definitive imaging
actions: Arrange compression ultrasonography for suspected DVT and CTPA or appropriate ventilation-perfusion imaging for suspected PE.
Give interim therapeutic anticoagulation when indicated by the approved pathway and imaging is delayed, after checking contraindications.
Obtain baseline blood count, renal and liver function, coagulation studies and pregnancy testing when relevant without delaying urgent treatment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently according to probability and stability

clinicalManagement.title: Start anticoagulation
actions: Select a locally formulary-approved anticoagulant based on renal and hepatic function, cancer, pregnancy potential, interactions, bleeding risk and patient preference.
Use generic agents and approved dosing references; do not derive dosing from this data record.
Document intended duration and the review point for extension or cessation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Once VTE is confirmed or interim treatment is indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Manage high-risk pulmonary embolism
actions: Activate critical-care and senior specialist support for haemodynamic instability.
Consider systemic thrombolysis or another reperfusion strategy only after rapid assessment of contraindications and local capability.
Provide respiratory and circulatory support while definitive therapy is organised.
Seek urgent haematology or vascular advice.
Consider a temporary mechanical strategy only when guideline criteria are met, with an explicit retrieval plan.
branches.condition: Anticoagulation is contraindicated

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Plan secondary prevention
actions: Classify the event as provoked, unprovoked or cancer-associated and document persistent risk factors.
Review adherence, interactions and bleeding precautions.
Avoid routine thrombophilia testing when it will not change management; seek specialist advice for selected cases.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before discharge

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review early after discharge for symptoms, bleeding, adherence and renal function where relevant; reassess treatment duration at the guideline-defined milestone and investigate persistent dyspnoea for post-PE complications.
mdtReferrals: Haematology for recurrent, unusual-site or selected unprovoked VTE
Oncology for suspected or active cancer-associated thrombosis
Vascular or interventional service for threatened limb or selected reperfusion decisions
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy or postpartum VTE
lifestyleAndDiet: Encourage mobilisation as tolerated once anticoagulation and clinical stability permit.
Reduce prolonged immobility during travel and recovery and maintain hydration when appropriate.
Address smoking, obesity and other modifiable vascular risks without implying that lifestyle replaces anticoagulation.
patientEducation: Explain clot symptoms, anticoagulant purpose, adherence and what to do after a missed dose using the medicine-specific approved information.
Provide urgent warning signs for recurrent PE and major bleeding.
Discuss procedure, dental and pregnancy-planning precautions before any anticoagulant change.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamics and oxygenation are stable and validated outpatient-risk criteria are met where outpatient care is proposed.
Anticoagulant access, renal-function appropriateness, administration and follow-up are confirmed.
Bleeding and recurrence precautions are understood and a responsible service owns pending results.

redFlags: Shock or severe dehydration
Reduced consciousness or inability to protect airway
Severe acidosis or dangerous potassium disturbance
Pregnancy or suspected cerebral injury
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Diabetic Ketoacidosis, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: More profound hyperosmolality and usually less prominent ketosis/acidosis; mixed presentations occur.
Exposure history and biochemical pattern differ.
May precipitate crisis or coexist; do not attribute all pain to DKA.

pathophysiology.summary: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketone production; osmotic diuresis produces water and electrolyte loss. Infection, interrupted insulin, new diabetes, medicines, or acute stress may precipitate crisis. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
